title.title: Quantitative trace-reconstruction bounds
title.subtitle: Claim: recovering an arbitrary $n$-bit string from random-deletion traces needs $n^{\Omega(\log\log n)}$ traces

plain: Recover a message from copies that each lost random letters: you need more copies than any power of its length

panels.caption: the hidden string; each bit is deleted independently
one trace: only the survivors, positions unknown

beats.text: Each bit is deleted with a fixed probability; you see only what survives
From many such traces, recover the whole string exactly
Claimed: the worst case needs $n^{\Omega(\log\log n)}$ traces

steps: Start with two words whose damaged copies nearly match
Nest copies with randomly flipped runs around them
Alternating sign patterns cancel what still differs
Repeat scale after scale until the difference is tiny

data.unit: each block: one scale of nesting
data.label: harder to tell apart at every scale

achievement.note: Also claimed: quasipolynomial upper bounds, down from $\exp(\tilde O(n^{1/5}))$

verify.detail: In Lean: the lower bounds only. Both quasipolynomial upper-bound papers are not
verify.ourCheck: We did not build the Lean or referee the proof

voice.text: How many damaged copies are needed?
Each copy loses random bits. How many copies recover the original?
Two strings nested scale after scale become nearly impossible to tell apart.
Claimed: more copies than any polynomial allows.

sources.quote: lower bound Omega~(n^{3/2}) by Chase ('New lower bounds for trace reconstruction', arXiv 1905.03031)
For every fixed deletion probability q in (0,1), exact worst-case reconstruction of an n-bit string from i.i.d. deletion traces needs n^{Omega(log log n)} traces
partial formalization: TraceReconstruction.lean covers the lower bounds only; both quasipolynomial upper-bound papers are unformalized
